title: Yowie on the Loose: undefeated week
excerpt: With Karl occupied as a witness in the Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial, you’ll have to wait another week for your dose of “the referee was right, actually“. Instead you get a players v RA pay dispute, 2027 Bledisloe news, gripping drama and some attitude from the second-worst Hansen. 31 Oct player pay dispute deadline looms
content:
With Karl occupied as a witness in the Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial, you’ll have to wait another week for your dose of “the referee was right, actually“. Instead you get a players v RA pay dispute, 2027 Bledisloe news, gripping drama and some attitude from the second-worst Hansen.

31 Oct player pay dispute deadline looms

Iain Payten of the SMH reports that the the deadline for a new collective bargaining agreement between Rugby Australia (RA) and the Rugby Union Players’ Association (RUPA) is only days away.

The belligerents have been at the table for months trying to strike a deal for a new five-year Commonwealth Bank of Australia collective bargaining agreement (CBA), with the current agreement expiring this Halloween (at which Hoss will be dress at himself, terrifying small children and adults alike).

RUPA is pushing for a significant pay increase for men’s and women’s players. It has also argued players should get a cut of the $100m fee coming to RA for co-hosting the men’s World Cup next year.

RA says it’s put up a good offer, with an uplift in minimum spend on players, and in bonuses for World Cup success.

RA argues it has a responsibility to not squander the big Lions and World Cup windfalls, and to use the money to secure the long-term future of the game in Australia. Some at RA were apparently stunned at the size of RUPA’s initial pay demands.

New RUPA boss Adrian “Ike” Turner, who took over in April, was formerly the head of legal at the Rugby League Players Association and he brought in another long-time RLPA figure, former Roosters and “fucken” Manly player Tom “Aussie Home Loans” Symonds, to become RUPA chief operating officer.

In 2023, when the RLPA and the NRL couldn’t reach a CBA deal by deadline, NRL stars then refused to do interviews with host broadcasters on match days (the lack of penetrating insight must have been devastating), delayed kick-off times and even taped over the NRL logo on their jerseys. There were threats to repeat their pay dispute boycott of the 2003 Dally M Awards, but that didn’t eventuate, with a deal finally struck after a month-long, mid-season standoff.

2027 Bledisloe test at MCG instead of somewhere nice

PlanetRugby reports that the Wallabies will face New Zealand at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (Saturday, 31 July) in a Bledisloe Cup Test as part of the Rugby Championship in 2027.

The latte-sipping commies will apparently also host an additional Bledisloe Cup Test match in 2029 as part of a new multi-year agreement between Rugby Australia and the Victorian Government.

Confirmation of the MCG Test completes an historic fixture list for the Wallabies in 2027, which begins with the first ever Bledisloe Cup Test on Anzac Day (at Suncorp Stadium, the best rugby venue in Australia). The year is then blighted by the aforementioned MCG game, followed by a third Test in New Zealand (venue TBC when the Kiwis figure out the old “arse vs elbow” difference).

The year concludes with the once-in-a-generation home Rugby World Cup. The Wallabies will meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup on 9 October 2027 at Accor Stadium (Homebush, although the sneaky New South Welsh appeared to have quietly created a new suburb called “Sydney Olympic Park”. The Wallabies and All Blacks will only meet again in 2027 if the ABs make the finals.

A crowd of 83,944 filled the MCG the last time the two sides met at the famous ground in 2023 – the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time – and 90,307 watched the Wallabies’ second Test against the British & Irish Lions last year, breaking the Lions’ all-time crowd record. None of said crowd could see what was going on due to the obvious-to-some limitations of a rectangle-field sport played in an oval stadium.

Tadhg Furlong cited over alleged Pat McGroin incident

Rugby365 reports that Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong could face a suspension after being cited for an alleged breach of conduct during Leinster’s United Rugby Championship victory over Munster at the Aviva Stadium.

Furlong was cited following an allegation that he grabbed Munster forward Phil McGoolies Gavin “Diddy” Coombes by the groin during the match. Coombes raised the incident with referee Andrew Brace, but television match official Colin Stanley was unable to find footage of the alleged incident.

The Leinster prop has been cited under Law 9.27, which states that players must not act against the spirit of good sportsmanship, including grabbing, twisting or squeezing an opponent’s genitals.

Furlong could face a sanction following a disciplinary hearing, with the outcome potentially affecting Ireland head coach Andy Farrell’s plans ahead of the resumption of the Nations Championship next weekend.

Munster coach Clayton McMillan backed Coombes over the allegation.

“All I know is that I back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn’t do it lightly,” McMillan said. “He’s not that sort of person, Gavin, so we’ll see where that goes.”

Steve Hansen sends shade back to Springbok fan

Planet Rugby reports that ‘attitude’ is definitely a club in the bag of former NZ coach Sir Steve “MMMbop” Hansen.

On the Rugby Unity podcast, host David Pembroke read out a letter from a fan who confidently stated what the difference is between South Africa and New Zealand at the moment.

“There is a clear understanding in the Springboks coaching squad; there is a certain way in which they deal with problems, and there is a certain way they conduct themselves about selection and what they need from each and every individual,” the letter read.

“They don’t just select their best players; they select players according to what that certain position requires. They give every player the blueprint and the opportunity to go back and study that blueprint.”

“Whereas the All Blacks just pick anyone who can score, offload and run into space. There is a lot of confusion on who plays where, what’s their role in the team.

“That’s where the real difference is between the teams. Scrums and all of that is just the icing on the cake.”

Hansen responded:

“I think it’s great, just keep watching this space and we’ll see what happens.”

“Passionate fans, I find, have got very short memories and they forget that those people we were picking off the street used to beat South Africa every time we used to play them a few years ago.”

“Right now, he doesn’t care about that, he just cares that they’re winning right now and that’s great, and I support him wholeheartedly.”

“That’s what makes rugby such a lovely thing, which is the fans. They get stuck in and they come up with all these theories, but the thing about a fan’s theory is it’s never tested.”

“You don’t have to test it, so you can say whatever you like.”
